[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"SavedModel Format and Serialization in TensorFlow"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to SavedModel"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"The SavedModel format is the standard serialization format for TensorFlow models. It is language-neutral, recoverable, and dense, making it ideal for production environments such as TensorFlow Serving, mobile devices, and custom runtimes."},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Contains a complete TensorFlow program, including trained weights and computation graphs."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Does not require original model source code to load and execute predictions."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Supports multiple MetaGraphs, allowing versioning and serving distinct execution targets."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Directory Structure"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you export a model using the SavedModel format, TensorFlow creates a directory containing specific files and subdirectories:"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"saved_model.pb or saved_model.pbtxt: The serialized MetaGraphDef protocol buffer, which defines the computation graphs."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"variables/: A directory containing checkpoint files of the serialized variables."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"assets/: Optional folder for external files, such as vocabulary or tokenizer tables."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Saving a Model"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"To serialize a Keras model into the SavedModel format, use the tf.saved_model.save function or the built-in model.save method."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf

# Define a simple sequential model
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu', input_shape=(32,)),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')
])

model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

# Save the model to disk
export_path = './saved_model_example'
tf.saved_model.save(model, export_path)"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Loading and Serving the Model"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once serialized, you can reload the SavedModel using tf.saved_model.load. This returns an object that maintains the original signatures and functions."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf

# Load the SavedModel back into memory
imported_model = tf.saved_model.load('./saved_model_example')

# Access the default serving signature
inference_func = imported_model.signatures['serving_default']

# Run inference
import numpy as np
input_data = tf.constant(np.random.random((1, 32)), dtype=tf.float32)
predictions = inference_func(input_data)
print(predictions)"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Production"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always define explicit input signatures using @tf.function(input_signature=...) to prevent unexpected tracing overhead."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Validate the saved model using the command-line tool 'saved_model_cli' to inspect available signatures and input types."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keep asset paths relative to ensure portability across different deployment environments."}]
